articles.title: AI reveals a hidden chemical shortcut that could turn CO2 into fuel
articles.summary: Scientists used artificial intelligence to uncover nearly 10,000 chemical reactions involved in transforming carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals, revealing crucial pathways that traditional models had missed. The discovery dramatically improved predictions of CO2 conversion and uncovered a surprising hydrogen reaction that could inspire more efficient catalysts.
articles.content:
Scientists have uncovered thousands of previously overlooked chemical reactions that could help improve the conversion of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) into valuable fuels and industrial chemicals. By combining machine learning with advanced computer simulations, researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) identified 9,389 individual reactions occurring on a copper catalyst, revealing unexpected chemical pathways that conventional models had missed.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, could help scientists develop more effective catalysts for transforming CO 2 into useful products such as methanol. The research also uncovered a surprising way hydrogen can participate in these reactions, challenging established assumptions about how the process works.

One promising approach to recycling carbon dioxide is hydrogenation, which uses a catalyst to help CO 2 react with hydrogen and form chemicals such as methanol. However, the process involves an enormous number of individual reactions taking place across the catalyst's surface. Simulating every possible step using quantum mechanics would require immense computing power, so researchers typically focus on a limited selection of reactions believed to be the most important. This simplification can leave hundreds of potentially critical reactions out of the picture.

"We began with a worry familiar to anyone who does mechanistic modeling: How do you know that your reaction network has not omitted the one step that matters?" says first author Anand Mohan Verma, who conducted the research as a CV Raman Postdoctoral Fellow at IISc and is now an Assistant Professor at the Motilal Nehru National Institute of Technology Allahabad (MNNIT Allahabad).

AI Reveals Thousands of Overlooked Chemical Reactions

To overcome this limitation, the research team began by using quantum mechanics simulations to build a detailed database containing 152 chemical reactions. They then trained machine learning models to quickly estimate the energy barriers that additional reactions would need to overcome.

Using automated computational tools, the scientists examined the possible reactions involving 105 chemical species present on the catalyst surface. They also determined which transformations could take place in a single reaction step. This approach expanded their original network from just 152 reactions to 9,389.

The difference was significant. When the researchers relied on the smaller network, their model incorrectly identified formic acid as the main product rather than methanol. It also predicted substantially less CO 2 conversion than experiments indicated.

"When we modeled the process using the 152 reactions considered initially, the network wrongly predicted formic acid, not methanol, as the major product, and underestimated how much CO 2 gets converted. Only when we expanded the network to include thousands of additional, previously overlooked reactions did the predictions fall in line with what we and others see experimentally," explains corresponding author Ananth Govind Rajan, Associate Professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering, IISc.

Expanded Model Predicts 40 Times More CO 2 Conversion

When the scientists incorporated the larger reaction network into a model of how quickly the chemical processes occur, the predicted amount of CO 2 conversion increased by approximately 40 times compared with the original model.

The expanded model also correctly identified methanol and carbon monoxide as major products, bringing its predictions into agreement with experimental findings.

Experimental validation was carried out by G Valavarasu and Santhosh Kotni at Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited's Green Research and Development Centre, along with Amol Amrute and colleagues at the Agency for Science, Technology, and Research in Singapore. Ambedkar Dukkipati, Professor in the Department of Computer Science and Automation at IISc, also contributed to the machine learning models.

A Surprising Hydrogen Pathway Challenges Conventional Chemistry

Beyond improving the predictions, the much larger reaction network exposed an unexpected mechanism involving hydrogen.

In several important reaction steps, hydrogen could be transferred to intermediate chemical compounds directly as molecular H2, rather than only through separate hydrogen atoms. Additional quantum mechanics calculations confirmed that this pathway can be especially favorable when hydrogen is transferred to intermediates containing oxygen.

This finding challenges a long-standing assumption about how hydrogen participates in catalytic reactions and could provide valuable clues for designing better catalysts.

"The idea that hydrogen can transfer as an intact molecule, without first splitting into atoms, runs against what most of us were taught," says co-author Shivam Chaturvedi, PhD student in the Department of Chemical Engineering, IISc. "This surfaced only because the network was large enough to allow for it, and the observation held up when we went back and computed those steps explicitly. This also suggests that catalysts that interact more strongly with H2 could potentially enhance pathways leading to methanol."

The researchers believe this unexpected mechanism could guide the development of catalysts that interact more effectively with molecular hydrogen, potentially improving the chemical pathways responsible for producing methanol from CO 2 .

The broader computational framework may also prove useful well beyond carbon dioxide hydrogenation. By integrating quantum mechanics simulations, machine learning, automated identification of chemical reactions, and models of reaction rates, the approach could help researchers investigate other important industrial processes.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough using AI to uncover thousands of previously unknown chemical reactions that improve the conversion of CO2 into valuable fuels like methanol. This discovery has broad environmental significance by advancing carbon recycling technologies, potentially reducing greenhouse gas emissions and reliance on fossil fuels. The research is detailed, focused, and validated experimentally, indicating a meaningful positive impact on climate action and sustainable energy.

articles.title: New team to save Antarctic port from climate change
articles.summary: The mission aims to protect the base which is home to the world’s southernmost Post Office.
articles.content:
A new team of UK specialists is embarking on a 9,000-mile journey to Antarctica to protect a British science base threatened by climate change.

The UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT), a Cambridge-based charity, is in its second year of a three-year mission to save Port Lockroy.

Its goal is to restore the site, which has the world's southernmost Post Office, museum, and more than 1,000 gentoo penguins.

This year's team will install beams and props to help the buildings withstand increased precipitation and snow loading, as well as monitor the penguins.

The site is more than 80 years old and faces structural deterioration due to rising temperatures and extreme weather on the rapidly warming Antarctic Peninsula.

After initial assessments revealed serious structural weaknesses, last year's team prepared the site ready for this season's interventions, which UKAHT said was the charity's "biggest ever conservation season" at Port Lockroy.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant conservation effort to protect an important Antarctic heritage site and its wildlife from the tangible impacts of climate change, with a broad environmental and scientific significance.

**What happened** – The UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT), a charity based in Cambridge, is in the second year of a three-year mission to save Port Lockroy. This year, a team of specialists traveled 9,000 miles to Antarctica to install beams and supports to strengthen the old buildings against heavy snow and rain. They are also monitoring the penguins living there.

**Impact** – The work is important because it helps protect a unique place that holds history and wildlife in one of the most remote parts of the world. Without these efforts, the buildings could collapse, and the penguin colony could be disturbed. This conservation project is the largest ever carried out by UKAHT at Port Lockroy.

**What's next step** – After this year’s repairs, the team will continue monitoring the site and penguins, and complete the restoration in the final year of the mission. The hope is to keep Port Lockroy safe for visitors, researchers, and wildlife for many years.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A UK team is working hard to protect an old Antarctic base and its penguins from climate change damage through a major conservation project.

articles.title: Scientists discovered the world’s largest octopus nursery off the California coast
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most of the deep seafloor is cold, dark, and barely mapped. The Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary covers more than 6,000 square miles of ocean along California’s central coast and is better studied than most of it. Even there, researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute somehow missed […]
The post Scientists discovered the world’s largest octopus nursery off the California coast first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Most of the deep seafloor is cold, dark, and barely mapped. The Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary covers more than 6,000 square miles of ocean along California’s central coast and is better studied than most of it. Even there, researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute somehow missed a gathering of 20,000 octopuses until 2018.

The site is now the largest known deep-sea octopus congregation on Earth, which raises an obvious question about what else is down there. It sits on a field of hydrothermal springs, and that’s the key. The springs warm the water above what the surrounding seafloor offers, which speeds up metabolism and egg development in the pearl octopuses (Muusoctopus robustus) drawn to the heat. Normally, female octopuses in the deep sea spend years brooding their eggs. At this site, they do it in about 1.8 years.

Why 20,000 octopuses gather here

Pearl octopuses are pale purple, roughly grapefruit-sized, and not especially known for company. Something about the thermal conditions here has drawn more than 20,000 of them to roughly 6.2 acres of seafloor. Using underwater mapping technology, researchers counted about 6,000 in a 2.5-hectare area and extrapolated the rest.

The dens they build use whatever is on the seafloor nearby: stones, shells, and whatever human objects have settled down there over time. After brooding their eggs, the females die, and their bodies become food for other animals in the area. The whole cycle keeps the local food web running on what the octopuses themselves leave behind.

What protection made this discovery possible

The octopus garden sits inside the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, which restricts oil and gas exploration, seabed mining, and other activities that can damage the seafloor. Hydrothermal fields in the deep sea are fragile and not well understood. Without protected status, this one could have been disturbed or destroyed before anyone knew what was living there.

This congregation went undetected until 2018 in one of the most closely monitored stretches of deep ocean in the world. Hydrothermal springs aren’t unique to this part of California, and the ocean has a lot of floor. The question the garden raises is how many other congregations, in thermal fields no one has mapped yet, are still down there.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.
articles.source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

It reveals a unique ecosystem sustained by hydrothermal springs that accelerates octopus reproduction, contributing to biodiversity and the health of the local food web. The protection of this area from damaging activities ensures the preservation of this fragile habitat, with implications for broader ocean conservation efforts.

articles.title: Why Google is paying to upgrade nuclear power plants
articles.content:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and WABE , Atlanta’s NPR station. ​

Last week, the Georgia Public Service Commission voted to approve a new deal between Georgia Power and the tech giant Google. Starting in 2028, Google will help pay for upgrades to the state’s nuclear reactors.

“So, around 100 megawatts of carbon-free energy, paid for by somebody else,” PSC Commissioner Stan Wise said to staffers shortly before the vote. “Why don’t you bring us some more of those deals?”

Georgia Power wants to upgrade four of the state’s older nuclear reactors at Plant Vogtle and Plant Hatch so they can produce more energy. State regulators approved the Vogtle upgrades last year, but the specifics of how to pay for the work weren’t hashed out. Now, the commission has voted to move ahead with the updates at Plant Hatch too — and approved a new subscription program so large customers like Google can pay for both.

“We appreciate Google’s continued leadership in this space and partnership in developing this program, which we see as the latest example of how large-load growth can benefit all electric customers,” said Aaron Mitchell, senior vice president of strategic growth for Georgia Power, in a statement.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Under the program, Google will pay a subscription fee on top of its electricity bill to help cover the cost of the nuclear upgrades. In exchange, Google gets credit toward its goal of using only carbon-free energy by 2030. Since nuclear plants don’t use fossil fuels, the power they generate qualifies; nuclear plants can also generate electricity around the clock, which solar and wind power can’t do.

Precise details of the agreement between Google and Georgia Power haven’t been made public. It’s expected to add 96 megawatts of nuclear capacity to the grid and provide “approximately $900 million in projected benefits to customers over the life of the units,” according to the utility.

“This collaboration with Georgia Power ensures that digital infrastructure growth goes hand-in-hand with positive local impact, helping to deliver hundreds of millions of dollars in direct customer benefits and supporting a more affordable, clean, and reliable energy system for all Georgia residents,” said Lucia Tian, director of advanced energy technologies for Google, in a statement.

Google also announced last week that it will partner with Constellation Energy to fund similar nuclear upgrades at reactors in Illinois, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania, adding 890 megawatts of energy to the grid for PJM, the largest grid operator in the country. Amazon has announced a deal to add capacity to a Constellation nuclear plant in Maryland.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Around the country, many utilities are meeting the boom in energy demand from hyperscale data centers by building new natural gas generation and extending the life of coal-fired power plants. Similarly, many data centers are building their own fossil-fuel generation. Deals like this one could present an alternative, according to Priya Barua of the Corporate Energy Buyers Association, which advocates for non-fossil energy solutions for corporate customers.

“A number of large energy customers are looking kind of across the board at what are all of the tools in the toolkit in order to actually support a reliable, affordable grid,” she said. “I do think we’re going to see a lot more of those types of innovations and thinking across the board.”

In addition to nuclear improvements like the ones in Georgia, those tools could include energy efficiency programs, transmission line upgrades, and efforts to reduce energy demand at key times to relieve pressure on the grid — all solutions that can be scaled up relatively quickly with an infusion of cash from a large tech company, Barua said. That speed could prove critical in the coming years because there are significant delays in the supply chain for natural gas turbines and other key components in the gas expansion that Georgia Power and other utilities are planning to meet data center demand. A new nuclear plant can take decades to build, whereas upgrading an existing plant can take around five years.

“It can mitigate delays in projects coming online,” said Katie Southworth, also of CEBA, of programs like the Google-Georgia Power deal. “You’ve got a relay race, and who is going to get to [commercial operation date] first. In order to have the resources to sort of run a competitive relay race, you have to have a lane for them to go into.”

articles.personality_title: Google partners with Georgia Power to upgrade nuclear plants for cleaner energy

Starting in 2028, Google will pay a subscription fee to support these improvements, which will add about 96 megawatts of clean energy to the grid.

**Impact** – This deal is important because nuclear energy does not produce greenhouse gases and can generate power all day and night, unlike solar or wind. By investing in nuclear upgrades, Google helps increase reliable clean energy for everyone in Georgia. The upgrades are expected to bring nearly $900 million in benefits to customers over the reactors’ lifetime.

**What’s next step** – Google will also support similar nuclear upgrades in other states like Illinois, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania. This partnership could encourage other big energy users to invest in clean energy projects, speeding up the transition to a more affordable and reliable energy system.
